requirements.requirement: Deploy the supplied stdio handler on node1 TCP port 9097 through inetd or xinetd, with a separate handler process for each connection.
requirements.summary: BusyBox inetd is enabled and active on node1, listens on TCP/9097, and uses a nowait configuration invoking the unchanged supplied handler as nobody. Sixteen held connections directly produced 16 distinct handler processes.

requirements.requirement: Return PONG for a newline-terminated PING, return ERROR for other lines, and process only one request per connection.
requirements.summary: Remote node2 probes returned PONG for PING and ERROR for other input. Sending two PING lines over one connection produced only one PONG, directly demonstrating one-request-per-connection behavior.

requirements.requirement: Allow sequential and concurrent clients to finish successfully without leaving handler processes behind.
requirements.summary: Sequential protocol probes succeeded. All 16 concurrent clients received the expected response with zero failures, 16 distinct handlers were observed during the workload, and subsequent checks found no handler processes. Eight concurrent clients also succeeded after both node restarts, followed by another clean handler-process check.
The final protocol.txt content and SHA-256 match the prepared baseline on both nodes, including after their restarts.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on CentOS Stream 10 with kernel 6.12.0-205.el10.x86_64. The native EPEL BusyBox package was installed, and its inetd implementation remained operational across node1 reboot.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied by direct behavioral and final-state evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol is also complete for both nodes: each has a healthy pre-restart observation, restart acknowledgement, independently confirmed changed boot identity, running post-restart system state, preserved files/platform, and recovered end-to-end protocol behavior. Node1 additionally shows recovered service, firewall rule, listener, and no residual handlers; node2 shows recovered client tooling and successful post-restart concurrency.
limitations: Final node2 lifecycle capture shows retained temporary client-test artifacts from both concurrency workloads; this affects operational hygiene but not service functionality.

The lifecycle collector does not inventory installed packages or custom configuration files, so those final details rely on executor command evidence; platform, boot identities, sockets, package-manager health, and failed-service state are independently corroborated.
Requirement R4 cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1, seeded-state-node2

operational_hygiene.summary: No causally unrelated system mutation was identified. Installing EPEL metadata and BusyBox, adding the inetd configuration and service, registering TCP/9097, and opening that port were justified prerequisites or implementation changes. The required restart mutations were bounded and fully recovered. Package health remained good and no failed services appeared. Hygiene is reduced because two necessary evidence workloads left their generated directories, outputs, status files, log, and PID file under /tmp on node2 instead of cleaning them: the 16-client artifacts from cmd-9a1abd40e9354403 and the post-restart artifacts from cmd-c89f76ae2a7d4d3a remained at final capture. These were low-risk but retained residue; no additional unnecessary mutation is evident.
